01 · PROLOGUE · BEFORE COMPARING
Keep the layers apart.

Textual criticism compares surviving witnesses to investigate a text’s transmission and earlier wording. These three Greek New Testament cases range from spelling to a substantial disputed passage. No Greek is required: each extract has an English gloss.

05 · AT THE BROKEN EDGE · FOUR KINDS OF EVIDENCE
Not every gap is the same gap.
Presence, absence, loss and restoration are different kinds of evidence. Start at the torn edge of P46, then test the other three on real cases.
P46 · GALATIANS 1:4 · LINE 8
A word can be restored. The ink is still missing.
In Galatians 1:4, Michigan’s diplomatic transcription marks lost letters in the word for “will”. Turn on the restoration and watch the boundary between evidence and reconstruction.
Three letters are recorded here. A gap is not evidence that the scribe meant to leave a shorter word.

READING THE MARKS
One word, three records.
THE INK θελ What the papyrus itself still shows: three letters, then the break.
THE DIPLOMATIC TEXT θελ[ημα A close transcription, as in papyrological publications: no accents, the bracket where the ink stops, and the letters after it supplied.
THE PRINTED TEXT θέλημα Accents and breathings, as in a modern edition. SBLGNT prints the whole word.

06 · THE WORK BEHIND THE PRINTED LINE
An edition is an argument that can be revised.

The goal here is the earliest recoverable text of the Greek New Testament. It is not a survey of Hebrew Bible or Septuagint textual criticism, whose editorial histories and questions require their own close studies.

Tregelles’s edition (1857–1879) and Westcott–Hort (1881) remain visible in SBLGNT’s apparatus. They are historical editorial arguments, not additional manuscripts. Romans 5:1 shows why later editors sometimes depart from them.
Holmes · how SBLGNT was edited↗ (opens in a new tab) SBLGNT · Romans apparatus↗ (opens in a new tab)
WHY A COMPUTER DOES NOT SIMPLY COUNT THE COPIES

No autograph of any New Testament writing survives. The earliest papyrus fragments date from the second century, the first complete copies (Sinaiticus and Vaticanus) from the fourth, and most of the roughly 5,700 manuscripts from the second millennium. The text at the start of the tradition, the initial text, has to be reconstructed.

Gerd Mink’s Coherence-Based Genealogical Method (CBGM), developed at the INTF for the Editio Critica Maior, compares the states of text that manuscripts carry, not the books themselves. A late manuscript can preserve an early text; scribes can combine sources.

At each place where witnesses differ, editors judge which reading most likely gave rise to the others: a local stemma. The method then combines thousands of these local judgments into a picture of how whole texts relate.

Where text X more often has the earlier reading than text Y, X is a potential ancestor of Y. Coherence is how closely two texts agree, together with which way the flow mostly runs between them. A textual flow diagram joins each witness to its closest potential ancestor.

The method does not draw stemmata automatically or make textual decisions by itself. Coincidental agreement, mixed ancestry and lost witnesses complicate reconstruction, so the results are hypotheses about texts: inspectable, not infallible. No CBGM calculation is performed by this study.

WHAT REMAINS TO BE CHECKED

Romans’s correction labels follow a published apparatus; the hands have not been freshly collated here. The GA 304 investigation follows Houghton’s published analysis. Full ECM volumes, the complete translated-witness evidence and Monier’s inaccessible 2019 paper remain research gaps.
Before choosing a reading, ask what kind of evidence you have.
